key_insight: A 127-qubit IBM Eagle processor can run end-to-end 10-class MNIST classification, but the practical win is workflow feasibility rather than a quantum accuracy advantage.
engineering_relevance: The paper shows how to reduce NISQ training overhead by training mostly off-hardware and using quantum multi-programming to boost inference throughput on real devices.
method: Two-phase training: classical gradient-based optimization for the encoder/readout, then gradient-free optimization for quantum parameters.
Use a trained quantum classifier for on-hardware inference instead of costly parameter-shift training on the device.
Apply Quantum Multi-Programming to pack multiple circuit copies on one processor for parallel inference.
evidence_signal: The authors benchmarked 10-class MNIST on IBM Eagle and compared against a matched-capacity classical network; they report no measurable accuracy gain from on-hardware fine-tuning and no mean-accuracy loss from multi-programmed inference.
watch_item: Performance is limited by NISQ noise and the absence of a per-parameter accuracy advantage at this scale, so hardware-specific results may not generalize.
paper_title: Image Classification on IBM Quantum Computers
